common_name: Sir Watkin Daffodil (The Welsh Peerless, Historic Giant Large-Cupped Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sir Watkin, nicknamed the Welsh Peerless, is a giant Victorian-era large-cupped daffodil named for Welsh landowner Sir Watkin Williams-Wynn.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in fall, in a site with full sun to light shade. Sir Watkin, nicknamed the Welsh Peerless, is a historic Division 2 large-cupped daffodil raised before 1868 and named for the Welsh landowner and politician Sir Watkin Williams-Wynn; it earned the Royal Horticultural Society's First Class Certificate in 1884. Its broad, soft sulphur-yellow petals arch gracefully around a deep, fluted golden cup, fading paler in strong sun, giving a goblet-shaped flower considered exceptionally large for its era and remained commercially important for decades. Allow foliage to die back fully after bloom and leave clumps undisturbed for several years to build strong flowering-size bulbs.

common_name: Empress Daffodil (Historic Backhouse Bicolor Giant Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Empress was bred by William Backhouse and introduced in 1869 alongside the related trumpet daffodil 'Emperor'.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Empress was bred by William Backhouse and introduced in 1869 alongside the related white-and-gold trumpet 'Emperor', together helping launch the Victorian craze for large-flowered trumpet daffodils. It carries a broad, pure white perianth surrounding a long, narrowly funnel-shaped, ribbed, rich yellow trumpet, a striking two-toned combination considered one of the finest bicolor trumpets of its time. It remains available today chiefly through heirloom bulb specialists as a historic garden daffodil. Deadhead spent blooms if desired and let the foliage die back naturally to recharge the bulb for next season.

common_name: Mrs. Langtry Daffodil (Historic Small-Cupped Bicolor Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Mrs. Langtry was raised by English breeder William Backhouse and named in 1869.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Mrs. Langtry is a historic Division 3 small-cupped daffodil raised by English breeder William Backhouse and named in 1869; it bears broad, slightly twisted ivory-white perianth segments surrounding a small, shallow cup that opens pale yellow and fades to near white, giving a delicate, old-fashioned look distinct from modern short-cupped hybrids. It blooms in mid-to-late spring on sturdy stems and is one of the longest-surviving named daffodils still offered by heirloom bulb specialists. Leave the foliage to die back fully after flowering for best rebloom the following spring.

common_name: Will Scarlett Daffodil (Historic Engleheart Red-Cupped Large-Cupped Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; bred by Rev. George Engleheart and registered before 1898, famous for an early record bulb sale price.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Will Scarlett was bred by the pioneering English clergyman-hybridizer Rev. George Engleheart and registered before 1898; when he exhibited it at Birmingham that year, three bulbs reportedly sold for a record-setting 100 pounds. This historic Division 2 large-cupped daffodil carries a wide, pure white perianth and a comparatively flat, frilled cup that opens yellow-orange and deepens to a fiery red-orange as the flower matures, a color combination rare for its period and influential on later red-cupped breeding. It remains prized by heirloom and historic daffodil collectors. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely after flowering before cutting it back.

common_name: Binkie Daffodil (Tasmanian Color-Changing Sulphur-to-White Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; bred by Guy L. Wilson and W. Wolfhagen in Tasmania, prized for its flower color shifting from pale yellow to near white as it ages.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in fall. Binkie was bred by Guy L. Wilson and W. Wolfhagen in Tasmania and is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil grown for its unusual reverse-bicolor behavior: the flower opens with a pale greenish-yellow perianth and a deeper, funnel-shaped pale yellow cup, then both fade together over several days to nearly pure white, with only a thin band of bright greenish-yellow persisting at the cup's rim. This slow color shift means a single planting shows several tones at once in cool spring weather. Grow in full sun to light shade and allow foliage to die back fully after bloom to sustain strong flowering in following years.

common_name: Golden Spur Daffodil (Historic All-Yellow Dutch Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; reputedly found on a private estate in Wassenaar, Holland, and in cultivation by 1885.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Golden Spur is a historic Division 1 trumpet daffodil of unrecorded Dutch parentage, reputedly found growing on a private estate in Wassenaar, Holland, and in cultivation by 1885. It bears a self-colored, rich golden-yellow perianth and a long, flanged trumpet of the same deep yellow, an entirely uniform golden flower rather than the bicolor effect common among trumpet daffodils of its time. Early American daffodil writer A.M. Kirby praised it in 1907 as one of his favorite cultivars, and it remains a vigorous, early-to-midseason heirloom for naturalizing in beds and borders. It multiplies steadily if left undisturbed for several years.
sources: DaffSeek / Royal Horticultural Society Daffodil Register

common_name: Cornish Chuckles Daffodil (Fragrant Multi-Headed Miniature Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; bred by Harry I. Tuggle Jr. in Virginia from 'Matador' x N. cyclamineus, first flowering in 1973.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Cornish Chuckles is a Division 12 (Miscellaneous) daffodil bred by Harry I. Tuggle Jr. in Virginia from a cross of 'Matador' and Narcissus cyclamineus, first flowering in 1973; it carries several small, rounded, lemon-yellow flowers with a deeper golden-yellow cup and lightly flecked petal tips on each sturdy stem, along with a light, sweet fragrance. Long popularized through Cornwall daffodil specialist nurseries, it remains a popular modern garden and cut-flower variety thanks to its compact habit and reliable multi-flowered stems. It performs best in free-draining soil and full sun; leave it undisturbed for several years to build up clumps.

common_name: Insulinde Tulip (Antique Virus-Broken Rembrandt-Group Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall; Insulinde is a genuine antique virus-broken Rembrandt-group tulip in commerce since before 1915, flamed violet-purple and bronze over a soft yellow ground.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in a site with sharp winter drainage, isolated from other prized tulips. Insulinde is a genuine antique broken tulip in commerce since before 1915, its irregular violet-purple and bronze flaming over a soft yellow-to-white ground caused by the historic tulip-breaking virus rather than bred-in pigment, the same naturally occurring mutation that drove Dutch Golden Age tulip mania. Because the virus is transmissible by aphids to other tulips, it is grown today only by specialist heirloom-bulb nurseries and should be kept apart from valuable unbroken cultivars. It flowers mid-to-late spring and multiplies slowly, making it a collector's plant rather than a mass-bedding tulip.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Absalon Tulip (Antique Virus-Broken Bizarre Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall; Absalon is a genuine antique virus-broken Bizarre-class tulip introduced in 1780, one of the oldest named tulip cultivars still in commerce.

directions: Set bulbs four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall, isolated from other prized tulips. Absalon is one of the oldest surviving named tulip cultivars still in commerce, introduced in 1780 and belonging to the historic Bizarre class of broken tulips, whose irregular coffee-brown and burgundy feathering, flaming, and marbling over a golden-yellow ground is caused by the same naturally transmissible tulip-breaking virus responsible for the famous Dutch tulip-mania patterns. It blooms in mid-to-late spring, is usually sourced from specialty heirloom-bulb growers, and should be planted away from unbroken tulip stocks since aphids can spread the virus.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Orange Emperor Tulip (Vivid Orange Fosteriana Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in fall; part of the Fosteriana 'Emperor' series, opening large vivid orange blooms very early in the season.

directions: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in well-drained soil. Orange Emperor belongs to the Fosteriana 'Emperor' series alongside the familiar red and white forms, opening extra-large, bright orange flowers on strong stems well ahead of mid-season tulips, with broad gray-green leaves typical of the group. Its bold color and early timing make it a popular companion for daffodils and other early bulbs in mixed spring displays. Fosteriana types tend to perennialize reasonably well in climates with cold winters, but bulbs should be treated as an annual planting where winters are mild or wet.
sources: John Scheepers Beauty from Bulbs — Fosteriana Tulip catalog
Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Ile de France Tulip (Vivid Scarlet Triumph Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in fall; a widely grown Triumph-division tulip valued for its saturated scarlet-red color and sturdy, weather-resistant stems.

directions: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in fertile soil with good winter drainage. Ile de France is a Triumph-division tulip, the largest and most commercially important tulip class, prized for its clean, saturated scarlet-red petals edged faintly yellow on compact, sturdy stems that stand up well to spring wind and rain. It flowers in mid-season, bridging the gap between early single and double tulips and the later Darwin Hybrid and lily-flowered types, and is a dependable choice for bedding, mass landscape color, and cutting. Like most Triumph tulips, flower size is typically best the first spring after planting.
sources: Longfield Gardens — Triumph Tulip variety listings

common_name: Persian Pearl Tulip (Magenta-Rose Species Tulip)

planting.note: Plant small bulbs three to four inches deep in fall; one of the earliest tulips to bloom, well suited to rock gardens and bulb lawns.

directions: Plant bulbs three to four inches deep in full sun to light shade in fall, in gritty, sharply drained soil. Persian Pearl is a selection of the dwarf species Tulipa humilis, opening fragrant, star-shaped flowers in deep magenta-rose with a bright yellow center and a silvery sheen on the outside of the petals, among the earliest tulips to bloom each spring. Its short stature and clump-forming habit suit rock gardens, raised beds, and naturalizing in turf, and like other wildflower tulips it is deer-resistant and tends to multiply and persist for years without replanting. It wants a dry summer dormancy, so avoid irrigating the planting site once the foliage yellows.
sources: High Country Gardens — species tulip catalog

common_name: Prinses Beatrix Snow Crocus (Clear Blue Chrysanthus with Yellow Throat)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; named for a Dutch princess, opens clear sky-blue flowers with a bright yellow base and throat.

directions: Set corms 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in autumn in a sunny, sharply drained site such as a rock garden, raised bed, or lawn edge. Prinses Beatrix, named for a Dutch princess, bears up to four lightly fragrant, rounded flowers per corm in clear, uniform sky-blue with a contrasting golden-yellow base and bright yellow stamens, opening among grayish-green, silver-striped foliage in late winter to earliest spring, well before the larger Dutch crocuses. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom, and divide congested clumps every several years during summer dormancy.

common_name: Albus Showy Crocus (Pure White Fall-Blooming Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to very early fall in well-drained soil; a pure white, vigorous selection of the showy autumn crocus.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; like the species it blooms just weeks after planting. Albus sends up large, goblet-shaped flowers in pure white, faintly veined at the base, with prominent feathery orange-red stigmas, emerging leafless from bare soil in September and October ahead of the strap-like spring foliage. It is regarded as the most vigorous and reliable white form of the species for naturalizing in lawns and under deciduous trees. Keep the planting site on the dry side through summer dormancy to avoid corm rot.

common_name: Oxonian Showy Crocus (Dark Violet-Blue Fall Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to very early fall in well-drained soil; regarded as among the darkest-flowered selections of the showy autumn crocus.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun; flowers appear on bare ground weeks after planting, well ahead of the foliage. Oxonian opens relatively large, goblet-shaped flowers in a deep violet-blue with darker veining toward the petal tips and bright orange anthers, among the deepest-colored of the named speciosus selections. Like the species, it multiplies freely where summer soil stays on the dry side and is an excellent choice for naturalizing in lawns, rock gardens, and under deciduous trees.

common_name: Blue Magic Grape Hyacinth (Compact Sky-Blue Muscari with White Tips)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a compact aucheri selection with sky-blue florets edged white.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Blue Magic is a compact, early-blooming grape hyacinth that produces dense, conical racemes of small, rounded sky-blue florets rimmed in white, with slightly paler, sterile florets capping each spike, carrying the sweet grape-like scent typical of the genus. It blooms in mid-spring, somewhat ahead of the common Armenian grape hyacinth, and is well suited to rock gardens, border edges, and containers. Let the narrow foliage yellow and wither naturally after flowering.

common_name: Siberian Tiger Grape Hyacinth (Pure White Armeniacum Selection)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a pure white-flowered sport of the common Armenian grape hyacinth.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Despite its name, Siberian Tiger is a pure-white-flowered selection of the familiar Armenian grape hyacinth: its urn-shaped florets open from pale green buds into dense, fragrant, all-white racemes in mid-spring, set against somewhat less rampant foliage than the common blue form. It multiplies at a slower pace than the blue form, making it less prone to the self-seeding spread that can make ordinary Muscari armeniacum weedy in beds. Combine it with the standard blue form or with later tulips for contrast.

common_name: Rosea Twinleaf Squill (Pink-Flowered Alpine Scilla)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in humusy, well-drained soil in full sun to light woodland shade; a long-cultivated soft-pink form of the two-leaf squill.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Rosea bears slender spikes of small, starry, six-petaled flowers that open deep pink in bud and fade to a soft rosy-pink as they mature, with carnation-pink anthers, atop the same paired strap-like leaves as the blue species form. It is among the earliest squills to bloom, often appearing alongside snowdrops and winter aconite in very early spring. It naturalizes readily in woodland gardens, rock gardens, and under deciduous shrubs without becoming weedy.

common_name: King of the Blues Hyacinth (Historic 1863 Late-Flowering Navy-Blue Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil; introduced in 1863, one of the oldest Dutch hyacinth cultivars still available and among the latest to bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Introduced in 1863, King of the Blues is one of the oldest Dutch hyacinth cultivars still available, carrying slender, old-fashioned, loosely set spikes of deep navy-blue, intensely fragrant florets. It is one of the latest hyacinths to bloom, flowering after most other cultivars have finished and helping extend the hyacinth season in mixed spring borders. Bulbs can be lifted and divided every few years if clumps become congested, and foliage should be left to die back fully after bloom.

common_name: Lady Derby Hyacinth (Historic 1883 Soft Rose-Pink Dutch Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil; available since 1883, a heirloom Dutch hyacinth with dense spikes of soft rose-pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Available since 1883, Lady Derby carries dense, upright spikes of large, intensely fragrant, soft rose-pink florets over a bloom period of two to three weeks, among the longer-lasting displays in the genus. Although it has faded from mainstream Dutch bulb trade listings over time, it remains available through heirloom and specialty bulb nurseries that preserve historic hyacinth cultivars. Grow it as for any Dutch hyacinth, and allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely after flowering before removing it.

common_name: L'Innocence Hyacinth (Ivory-White Award of Garden Merit Dutch Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil; a long-popular ivory-white Dutch hyacinth that holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 5-6 inches apart in fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. L'Innocence produces dense, cylindrical spikes of very fragrant, bell-shaped, ivory-white florets along stout, fleshy stems in early to mid-spring, and is one of the most widely grown white hyacinth cultivars for garden display, forcing, and cut flowers alike. It has long been recognized with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance. Deadhead spent spikes if desired but leave the foliage in place until it yellows naturally.

common_name: Walrus Snowdrop (Double Snowdrop with Long Twisted Tusk-Like Petals)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; named by galanthophile Oliver Wyatt in the 1960s for its long, twisted outer petals resembling walrus tusks.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Walrus is a double-flowered selection of the common snowdrop, named by English galanthophile Oliver Wyatt in the 1960s for its three unusually long, narrow, mostly green outer segments that curve outward and downward like a walrus's tusks, surrounding a dense rosette of smaller, strongly green-marked inner petals. It is a slow-to-establish, slow-to-multiply collector's snowdrop best appreciated at close range in a trough, raised bed, or path-side planting. Lift and divide congested clumps in the green immediately after flowering for best transplant success.

common_name: Grumpy Snowdrop (Frowning-Faced Poculiform Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; discovered by galanthophile Joe Sharman in the Cambridge garden of polar explorer Sir Vivian Fuchs.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Grumpy was discovered by galanthophile Joe Sharman in the Cambridge garden of polar explorer Sir Vivian Fuchs and is prized for the green markings on its inner petals, which merge into a single bold blotch that, viewed face-on, resembles a scowling or frowning face. It is an elegant, narrow-flowered, upright, vigorous grower with narrow leaves, though it multiplies more slowly than many named snowdrops, which has kept it a sought-after novelty among collectors. Divide congested clumps in the green immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active.
sources: The Garden of Eaden (snowdrop grower account)

common_name: Ophelia Snowdrop (Greatorex Double Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; one of Heyrick Greatorex's Shakespeare-named double snowdrops, bred in Norfolk.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Ophelia, named for the Shakespearean character, is one of the earliest-flowering Greatorex double snowdrops, bred by Heyrick Greatorex in Norfolk, England, by crossing Galanthus nivalis and G. plicatus. It produces a neat, well-rounded double flower with narrow outer segments faintly tipped green and a densely packed center of about a dozen smaller inner petals marked with a bold green U-shape. It is a reliable, quick-to-bulk-up grower typically flowering in late February, well suited to a woodland or shaded border alongside hellebores and other early bulbs.

common_name: Cowhouse Green Snowdrop (Heavily Green-Striped Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; discovered in Susan Cowdy's garden in Rushmere, Buckinghamshire, in the 1980s.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Discovered in Susan Cowdy's garden in Rushmere, Buckinghamshire, in the 1980s, Cowhouse Green is a tall-growing snowdrop valued for its distinct pale green stripes running down the outer petals along with bold markings and a pale green blush at the base of the inner segments, giving the whole flower a noticeably greener cast than a typical white-and-green snowdrop. It is a reasonably vigorous grower that bulks up into worthwhile clumps over a few seasons when left undisturbed.

common_name: Mighty Atom Snowdrop (Early Large-Flowered Vigorous Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; raised by John Gray and later named by E.B. Anderson after inheriting stock in 1952, valued for unusually large flowers and very early bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Originally raised by John Gray and later named and distributed by British plantsman E.B. Anderson after he inherited stock in 1952, Mighty Atom is a long-established garden snowdrop noted for producing surprisingly large, rounded, pure white flowers with a bold deep-green inverted-heart mark on the inner segments, carried on a comparatively short, compact plant. It is also valued for flowering unusually early, often beginning around the Christmas period and continuing into January in mild years, well ahead of most other named cultivars.

common_name: Pyrenean Fritillary

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, sharply well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; native to meadows and rocky slopes of the Pyrenees and northern Spain.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, sharply well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun for mid-spring bloom. Pyrenean fritillary carries one or two solitary, nodding, bell-shaped flowers checkered in dusky maroon-purple on the outside, opening to reveal a yellow-green interior when viewed from below. Native to mountain meadows and rocky slopes of the Pyrenees and northern Spain, it is a sturdy, relatively easy species fritillary that tolerates ordinary garden soil better than many of its showier Mediterranean relatives, making it a good choice for a rock garden, raised bed, or sunny border edge. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after flowering.

common_name: Assyrian Fritillary

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; native to dry stony slopes of Turkey, Iran, and Iraq, needs a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply well-drained, gritty or sandy soil in full sun for early to mid-spring bloom. Assyrian fritillary is a slender, dwarf species from the dry stony slopes and steppe of eastern Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and the Caucasus, bearing narrow gray-green leaves and one or two small, narrow, bell-shaped flowers in dusky maroon-brown with a thin, bright greenish-yellow rim at the recurved petal tips. Like many fritillaries from this arid region, it demands sharp drainage and a completely dry summer dormancy, and is best grown in a bulb frame, raised bed, or gravel garden rather than ordinary border soil where it is prone to rot.

common_name: William Rex Crown Imperial (Bronze-Orange Crown Imperial)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; carries bronze-orange flowers and stems often flushed dark bronze-purple.

directions: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, since standing water in the hollow-crowned bulb quickly causes rot. William Rex bears intense reddish-orange, bell-shaped flowers on dark bronze-colored stems to about 3 feet, with the flowers held more sideways than purely pendent, flowering for two to three weeks in April. As with other crown imperial selections, every part of the plant carries a musky, spicy scent that deters deer, voles, and other bulb pests. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering and avoid disturbing established clumps, since crown imperials resent being divided or moved.

common_name: American Onion (One-Leaf Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil; this western native tolerates heavier, moister soils than most ornamental onions.

directions: Native to open grassy slopes in California and Oregon, Allium unifolium produces loose, rounded umbels of rose-pink, star-shaped flowers atop slender stems in late spring. Unlike many Mediterranean and Central Asian ornamental onions, it tolerates somewhat heavier soil and more summer moisture without rotting. Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in full sun to light shade; it naturalizes readily by offsets and self-seeding in congenial sites. The single broad, strap-like leaf that gives the species its name withers as flowering begins.

common_name: Black-Flowered Garlic (Broad-Leaved Garlic)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this Mediterranean species is easy and long-lived once established.

directions: Allium nigrum bears a dense, rounded umbel of starry white to pale grayish-pink flowers, each with a small dark greenish-black ovary at its center that gives the species its common name. Native to the Mediterranean region and southwest Asia, it is an easy, reliably perennial garden onion that tolerates poor, dry soils and heat better than many showier hybrids. Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in full sun; the flattened umbels contrast well with the globe-shaped heads of A. giganteum and A. 'Globemaster' and attract bees and other pollinators in late spring.

common_name: Dark Allium (Balkan Ornamental Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in sharply drained soil; the deep maroon flowers are among the darkest of any ornamental onion.

directions: Native to the Balkans and western Asia, Allium atropurpureum produces loose, flattened umbels of small, star-shaped flowers in an unusually dark maroon-purple shade, among the darkest of any commonly grown ornamental onion. It is a parent species behind several deep-colored hybrid alliums and remains available in its own right from specialty bulb nurseries. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, since it is prone to rot in heavy, wet soils over winter. The dark color reads almost black in low light, making it a striking foil for silver-foliaged companions.

common_name: Forelock Allium (Egg-Shaped Maroon-Purple Ornamental Onion with Floral Topknot)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; a drumstick-onion selection with a shaggy tuft of green bracts topping each flower head.

directions: Forelock is a selection of the eastern Mediterranean drumstick onion Allium amethystinum, bearing egg-shaped umbels of tightly packed, fragrant maroon-purple florets on stems to two or three feet. As flowering progresses, a distinctive tuft of elongated floret segments protrudes from the top of the head like a forelock or topknot, and increasingly prominent white stamens create a pale haze over the dark flower as it matures. Plant bulbs in full sun in fall, in average, dry-to-medium well-drained soil; it is easy to grow and attracts bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. Leave the seed heads standing for continued interest after bloom.

common_name: Pinball Wizard Allium

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a cross of Allium macleanii and A. christophii, the same parentage as 'Globemaster', bearing some of the largest flower globes of any garden allium.

directions: Pinball Wizard is a giant-flowered ornamental onion bred from the same Allium macleanii x A. christophii cross that produced 'Globemaster', bearing dense, six-inch globes packed with silvery-lavender florets on stems reaching 24 to 30 inches, while still carrying some green foliage at bloom time. The massive flower spheres are carried on sturdy stems that hold up well without staking. Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and leave the dried seed heads standing for late-season structure in the border.

common_name: Silver Spring Allium

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; the creamy-white petals each carry a dark rose-purple eye that intensifies as the bloom matures.

directions: Silver Spring produces elegant, rounded umbels of creamy-white, star-shaped florets, each marked with a deep rose-purple eye at the center that intensifies as the bloom matures, giving the overall head a refined bicolor effect. Reaching 24 to 30 inches tall, it flowers in late spring to early summer and draws bees and other pollinators while offering strong deer resistance and excellent drought tolerance once established. Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in full sun and well-drained soil; it brings a soft, luminous accent to mixed borders, gravel gardens, and late-spring perennial plantings.
